summary:
This page is mostly figures.

**Figure 17.5, 'Grid of digits decoded from the latent space'**, is the 840 × 840 mosaic produced by Listing 17.6 (p.542): 900 white-on-black digits decoded from a 30 × 30 grid of points over [-1, 1]² in the VAE's 2D latent space. Reading from the top, broad bands of 7s give way to 9s and 4s, then 8s, 5s, 3s and 2s, with 6s and finally 0s filling the lower part and the right side. At every boundary the digits blend: a 3 gradually turns into a 5 or an 8, a 2 into a 6, a 6 into a 0. This is the 'completely continuous distribution' described on p.542.

**Figure 17.6, 'Image super-resolution'**, shows a photo of bananas and a fruit bowl twice. On the left is a 'Low-resolution image with artifacts' (blurry, blocky, with compression halos); an arrow points to the right, a 'Crisp high-resolution image'. It illustrates the super-resolution models introduced at the start of section 17.2.

The text then gives the key caveat. These models are **not magically recovering lost details hidden in the input**, as in the 'enhance' scene from *Blade Runner* (1982). They make **educated guesses** about what the image should look like: they are **hallucinating** a cleaned-up, higher-resolution version (the sentence finishes on p.544). This guessing is the key to the next step: if a model can plausibly invent missing detail, repeated application can invent an entire image.

paragraphs.excerpt: Of course, these models aren’t magically recovering lost details hidden in the input,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Super-resolution models do not recover lost details hidden in the input, as in the 'enhance' scene from Blade Runner (1982). They make educated guesses about what the image should look like: they hallucinate a cleaned-up, higher-resolution version (sentence continues on p.544).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Downsampling and compression destroy information: many different high-resolution images map to the same low-resolution one. No algorithm can tell which of them was the original. A trained model picks a plausible candidate based on the statistics of its training images. The output looks sharp, but its fine details are invented, not measured.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the conceptual bridge to diffusion. 'Hallucination' is usually a weakness, but for generation it is the whole point. A diffusion model hallucinates an image from pure noise by making such educated guesses many times (p.544). The paragraph also sets up the practical warning on p.544: AI-enhanced cameras can invent moon craters, so never use these models for forensics.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: super-resolution is an ill-posed inverse problem. If D is the degradation (downsample + compress), then D(x₁) = D(x₂) for many different x₁, x₂. A model trained with a pixel-wise L2 loss outputs roughly the average of all plausible x, which tends to look blurry. Models trained with perceptual, adversarial or diffusion objectives instead output one sharp sample from the plausible set, which looks realistic but is invented.

terminology.meaning: Producing plausible detail that was not present in the input, inferred from training data statistics.
The Blade Runner trope where a detective zooms indefinitely into a photo to reveal hidden detail, which is physically impossible from a fixed-resolution image.

concepts.name: Latent space
concepts.definition: The low-dimensional vector space a generative model samples from and decodes into images.
concepts.intuition: Figure 17.5 is a printed map of a 2D latent space: each position on the page corresponds to a position in the latent plane.
concepts.technical: The figure covers the square [-1, 1]² of the VAE's 2D latent space at a step of 2/29 per tile.
concepts.significance: A continuous latent space means new points decode to plausible images and paths decode to smooth morphs.
concepts.example: The transition region where 3s become 5s in the upper half of Figure 17.5.
concepts.misconception: That the class regions are separated by sharp borders. The figure shows gradual blends.

concepts.name: Image super-resolution
concepts.definition: Producing a higher-resolution, cleaner image from a low-resolution, possibly noisy one.
concepts.intuition: Filling in a coarse sketch with detail that matches what such scenes usually look like.
concepts.technical: An image-to-image network trained on (degraded, original) pairs; the missing high-frequency content is predicted, not recovered.
concepts.significance: Shipped in smartphone cameras (p.542); its 'educated guess' nature is what diffusion models exploit.
concepts.example: Figure 17.6: the blurry, artifact-laden fruit photo becomes crisp.
concepts.misconception: That the sharp output is the true scene. It is one plausible reconstruction.

concepts.name: Hallucination (in generative models)
concepts.definition: Generating content that looks plausible but is not supported by the input; here, invented image detail.
concepts.intuition: Like a sketch artist filling in a half-remembered face: confident, plausible and possibly wrong.
concepts.technical: When the inverse problem has many solutions, a model trained on image statistics outputs a high-probability one. Its details reflect the training distribution, not the specific scene.
concepts.significance: A failure mode for forensics (p.544) but the mechanism that lets diffusion models create images from noise.
concepts.example: A camera rendering crisp moon craters from a blurred printout (p.544).
concepts.misconception: That hallucination is just a bug to be eliminated. For generation it is exactly the desired behaviour, as long as it is plausible.

deeper.title: Why information cannot be 'enhanced' back
deeper.body: Beyond the book: take a 2 × 2 block of pixels with values (10, 30, 50, 70) and downsample it by averaging to one pixel with value 40. The blocks (40, 40, 40, 40), (0, 80, 0, 80) and (70, 10, 30, 50) also average to 40. From the single value 40 there is no way to know which block was there. A super-resolution model picks one, the block most typical of its training data in that context. For a 4× upscale each pixel must become 16, so the number of possible originals grows quickly with the factor.

deeper.title: Reading Figure 17.5 as a map
deeper.body: Each tile's position encodes its latent coordinates: column j has z[0] = -1 + 2j/29 and row i has z[1] = 1 - 2i/29 (Listing 17.6, p.542). So the figure is a map of the latent plane: the top band (7s) is the region of large z[1]; the bottom-right region of 0s is low z[1] / high z[0]. Blended digits mark the borders between class regions. Note (an observation from the image, not stated in the book): within this [-1, 1]² window, 1s are not clearly visible, so the 'one-ness' direction mentioned on p.542 likely points toward a region outside the plotted square.

deeper.title: A forensic sketch artist
deeper.body: A super-resolution model is like a sketch artist working from a blurry CCTV still. The drawing is crisp and believable, but the details (the exact eyes, the scar) come from the artist's knowledge of faces in general. That makes it great for making photos look good and dangerous as evidence, as the book warns on p.544.

misconceptions.claim: A sharper output from a super-resolution model proves the detail was in the input.
misconceptions.correction: The model makes educated guesses and hallucinates detail; the input does not contain enough information to determine it (p.543-544).

misconceptions.claim: Figure 17.5 shows digit classes in separate clusters with empty space between them.
misconceptions.correction: The figure shows continuous blending: every tile is a digit or an in-between shape, with no blank or garbage regions.

takeaways: Figure 17.5 is the output of Listing 17.6: digits decoded from a 30 × 30 grid over the VAE's 2D latent plane, blending continuously from class to class.
Figure 17.6 shows super-resolution turning a low-resolution, artifact-laden photo into a crisp one.
Super-resolution does not recover hidden detail; it makes educated guesses, i.e. it hallucinates a plausible clean image.
That guessing ability is what diffusion models exploit to generate images from pure noise.

questions.question: Why do the authors say super-resolution models are 'hallucinating' rather than recovering detail?
questions.answer: Because the low-resolution input does not contain the fine details; many high-resolution images are consistent with it. The model fills in the most plausible detail from what it learned on training images, which is an educated guess.
questions.explanation: The page states the models are 'making educated guesses about what the image should look like'. The information-theory reason (many-to-one degradation) is an added explanation.

questions.question: Which code listing produces Figure 17.5, and how many digits does it contain?
questions.explanation: The listing on p.542 sets n = 30 and decodes one digit per grid location.

questions.question: In Figure 17.5, what do you see at the boundary between two digit classes, and what does that tell you about the latent space?
questions.answer: Intermediate shapes that blend the two digits (e.g. a 3 turning into a 5). It shows the latent space is continuous: nearby points decode to similar images with no gaps.
questions.explanation: This is the 'completely continuous distribution' described on p.542.
